instructions: Is `test_code` a cosmetic happy-path permutation of a path whose real risk is a refusal or failure case — permissions, tenant isolation, duplicates, retries, concurrency, partial failure — that nothing in `sibling_tests` covers either?

Does `test_code` (with `file_context`) mock or stub the exact collaborator whose integration with the code under test is the thing being tested — both sides of a write/read, producer/consumer, authorization, persistence, cache-key, queue, signature or serialization boundary faked so they agree by construction?
Does `test_code` with `file_context` mock or stub so many collaborators that the only real code left running is glue, so a wiring or contract bug between the real components could not be observed?

Procedure. 1. List every refusal or failure branch in `implementation`: authorization and tenant guards, duplicate or already-used rejections, version/concurrency conflicts, quota and limit caps, retry exhaustion, rollback on partial failure, over-amount money guards. 2. Name the riskiest one. 3. Search `test_code` and every `sibling_tests` name for that exact condition. A sibling covering a different branch — unknown id, not found, expiry, bad input, empty result — does not count. Answer yes when the riskiest branch is exercised by nothing. Answer no when this block or a sibling drives it, or `implementation` has no refusal branch.
Does `test_code` pass when an unexpected error is swallowed, logged or answered with a fallback, or use try/catch in a way that also passes when nothing throws at all?

Name the behaviour the test title claims — a refusal, a signature match, single-use, atomicity, a key agreeing. In `implementation`, find which collaborator decides it. Is that collaborator replaced in `test_code` by a scripted mock, so the asserted outcome is just what the mock was told (or two fakes tuned to agree)? Answer no when only neighbours are faked — signer, mailer, notifier, clock, metrics, downstream HTTP — and the asserted values, including the arguments handed to those fakes, are computed by real code, or real code's own branch is why a fake went uncalled.

List the collaborators the `implementation` actually calls — imported modules, injected objects. Ignore objects built in `test_code` that never reach it. Answer yes when the faked collaborators include first-party code (repositories, stores, ORM or transaction handles, policy or rule modules, hooks, helpers) and what stays real is glue — returning a stub's value, interpolation, arithmetic, assembling stub returns — so no two real components could disagree. Two faked collaborators can be enough. Answer no when only true external edges are faked (clock, randomness, HTTP, third-party gateway, filesystem) and real logic computes the asserted value.

Name the behaviour the test title claims — a refusal, a match, single-use, atomicity, a write landing, a key agreeing. In `implementation`, find which collaborator decides it. Smell if that collaborator is a scripted mock in `test_code`: the asserted outcome is what the mock was told, its canned read cannot reflect the write, or the only evidence is that it was called. No when just neighbours are faked — signer, mailer, clock, metrics, downstream HTTP — and the asserted values, including arguments passed to them, come from real code, or real code's own branch kept a fake uncalled.

Is this test's green independent of the specific failure it claims to cover? Decide in order: (1) `test_code` exercises no refusal, invalid input, failure or fallback path at all → no. (2) Its expects sit inside a test-side try/catch or `.catch()` and nothing (`expect.assertions`, `rejects.`, a throw at the end of the try) forces them to run → yes, however specific the matcher inside. (3) The error matcher accepts any error: bare `toThrow()`/`rejects.toThrow()`, `toThrow(Error)`, `toBeInstanceOf(Error)`, `toBeDefined()`, or a lone `not.toThrow()` → yes. (4) `implementation` funnels every exception on that path into the asserted value — null, [], false, `ok:false`, defaults, a cached value, status 200, an error count or length, a logged line, a counter → yes. Else no.

Is most of the setup in `test_code` and `file_context` unrelated to the behavior under test, so that the actual assertion is hard to find?

Inventory everything `test_code` and `file_context` construct: `vi.mock` calls, top-level consts, fixture objects and their fields, inserted records. Then trace the asserted call through `implementation`: which of those does the exercised path actually read, so that changing it would change the asserted value? Is most of that setup inert — deletable without touching the assertion?

criteria.true: Most mocks, fixtures or fields never reach the asserted value; they exist to make the test look realistic.
criteria.false: Every fixture and mock is read by the exercised path or named in an assertion — or the setup is only a few lines, whatever else is wrong with the test.

Does `test_code` test framework or component internals and implementation details — React state, private methods, CSS class names, source text, statement order — instead of user-visible or externally observable behavior?

Name the contract surface in `implementation`: return values, thrown errors, rendered text/roles/labels/aria/disabled/href, state read back out of storage, payloads handed to callbacks or collaborators. Answer no when `test_code` asserts on that surface â a class string that is the function's own return value counts, as does a storage round-trip. Answer yes when the asserted value is reachable only by peeking: private members or React state via an any-cast, instance or ref; class names, tag names or child counts of rendered DOM; render or stubbed-child call counts; source text; internal step or action-type order; or the shape or size of a table or bookkeeping accessor whose consuming function in `implementation` is never called.
Would `test_code` still pass if the behavior its name (`test_name`, under `describe_path`) describes were broken in an obvious way in `implementation`?

Read `test_name` (under `describe_path`) as a promise about one branch or guard in `implementation`. Procedure: name that branch; trace this fixture through `implementation` and ask whether it reaches the branch's live side, or whether an earlier return, a default, a fallback, or a second path that matches produces the same asserted values; then delete the branch and re-run the fixture. Yes if every assertion still holds.

Yes if every assertion still holds. No when the assertions pin the exact output the named behavior itself produces.

Is the code under test in `test_code` and `implementation` a small pure primitive — a formatter, getter, trivial mapper, constant lookup or thin wrapper — whose bugs would be obvious in any wider test of the feature that uses it?

First: was the EXPECTED side of the assertion produced by the implementation running during this test, or is it a stored artifact — read from disk, a committed/golden file, a fixture, a snapshot? Stored artifact, or the inverse operation (decoding what was encoded, verifying what was signed), or a literal: answer no, that is a drift/parity guard. Otherwise answer yes when the test builds the expectation by re-running the same formula, loop, or production helper the `implementation` uses on the same input, so a wrong algorithm is wrong identically on both sides.

Yes if every assertion still holds.

Find in `implementation` the body of the function this test calls, and judge that body, not how short the test is. Yes only if it is one return expression or forwards to a single call — a lookup, getter, template string, one-line map/filter/sort, or thin wrapper — where a single `??`, `||` or ternary default still counts as trivial. No if it loops, branches more than once, uses a regex, parses or formats input, resolves paths, files or module specifiers, dedupes, caps or truncates, does date or rounding arithmetic, or checks permissions.

Judge the body, in `implementation`, of the function the test calls — not how short the test is. Yes if it is one expression, a thin wrapper, or a switch or table returning constants; a single `??`, `||` or ternary default stays trivial. No if it loops, uses a regex, parses or formats input, resolves paths, files or module specifiers, dedupes, caps or truncates, does date or rounding arithmetic, or checks permissions. Also no when the test builds its inputs through other real production code — a factory, validator or constructor — since more than the primitive then runs.

Does `test_code` reproduce the algorithm under test — the same formula, loop, or production helper `implementation` uses — to construct what it asserts (the expected value, or an input engineered to satisfy it), so test and implementation would share the same mistake instead of a fixed, requirement-derived example? Answer no when the comparison is a drift or parity guard rather than a recomputation: one side is a stored artifact (a committed/golden file read from disk, a checked-in fixture, a snapshot) that generator output must match, or it round-trips an inverse operation (decode what was encoded, verify what was signed).
